His all-too-timeless speed. {{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 43.}}</poem>
He kindles anger by ''untimely'' jokes.
{{right|''Crabbe'', Tales, Works, IV. 8.}}}}
(''c'') Happening before the natural time; premature: as, ''untimely'' death; ''untimely'' fate.
{{smaller block|The ''untimely'' fall of virtuous Lancaster.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., i. 2. 4.}}}}

'''untimely''' (un-tīm′li), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''untimeliche''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''timely'', ''adv.''] In other than the natural time; unseasonably.
{{smaller block|Can she be dead? Can virtue fall ''untimely?''
{{right|''Fletcher'', Humorous Lieutenant, iv. 2.}}}}

'''untimeous, untimeously,''' ''adv.'' See ''untimous'', etc.

'''untimous''' (un-tī′mus), ''a.'' [Also ''untimeous''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''timous''.] Untimely; unseasonable: as, ''untimous'' hours.
{{smaller block|Of ''untymous'' persons: He is as welcome as water in a rivin ship. He is as welcome as snaw in harvest.
{{right|''Ray'', Proverbs (1678), p. 377.}}
His irreverent and ''untimeous'' jocularity.
{{right|''Scott'', Quentin Durward, I. 304.}}
[The knock] was repeated thrice ere . . . [he] had presence of mind sufficient to inquire who sought admittance at that ''untimeous'' hour.
{{right|''Barham'', Ingoldsby Legends, I. 72.}}}}

'''untimously''' (un-tī′mus-li), ''adv.'' [Also ''untimeously''; < ''untimous'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] In an untimous manner; untimely. ''Scott'', Kenilworth, xv.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|unthrift|6651|unto}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''unthrift''' (un-thrift′), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [< ME. ''unthrift''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''thrift''.] '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' Lack of thrift; thriftlessness; prodigality.
{{smaller block|<poem>For youthe set man in alle folye,
In ''unthrift'' and in ribaudie.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 4926.}}}}
{{smaller block|A hater of folly, idleness, and ''unthrift''.
{{right|''Harper’s Mag.'', LXXVI. 805.}}}}

'''2†.''' Folly.
{{smaller block|He roghte noght what ''unthrift'' that he seyde.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 431.}}}}

'''3.''' A prodigal; one who wastes his estate by extravagance; one without thrift.
{{smaller block|Hauing his sonne and heire a notable ''vnthrift'', & delighting in nothing but in haukes and hounds, and gay apparrell.
{{right|''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 235.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>To behold my door
Beset with ''unthrifts'', and myself abroad?</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Case is Altered, ii. 1.}}}}

'''II.†''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Profuse; prodigal.
{{smaller block|What man didst thou ever know ''unthrift'' that was beloved after his means?
{{right|''Shak.'', T. of A., iv. 3. 311.}}}}

'''2.''' Poor; unthrifty.
{{smaller block|[He] hath much adoo (poore penniefather) to keepe his ''unthrift'' elbowes in reparations.
{{right|''Nashe'', Pierce Penilesse, p. 8.}}}}

'''unthriftihead†''' (un-thrif′ti-hed), ''n.'' [< ''unthrifty'' + ''-head''.] Unthriftiness.
{{smaller block|Unquiet Care and fond ''Unthriftyhead''.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. xii. 25.}}}}

'''unthriftily''' (un-thrif′ti-li), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''unthriftily''; < ''unthrifty'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] '''1.''' Poorly.
{{smaller block|They been clothed so ''unthriftily''.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Canon’s Yeoman’s Tale, l. 340.}}}}

'''2.''' In an unthrifty manner; wastefully; lavishly; prodigally.
{{smaller block|Why will you part with them [names] here ''unthriftily?''
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Epigrams, vii.}}}}

'''unthriftiness''' (un-thrif′ti-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being unthrifty; prodigality.
{{smaller block|Staggering, non-proficiency, and ''unthriftiness'' of profession is the fruit of self. {{right|''Rogers'', Naaman the Syrian.}}}}

'''unthrifty''' (un-thrif′ti), ''a.'' [< ME. ''unthrifty''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''thrifty''.] '''1.''' Profitless; foolish; wretched.
{{smaller block|Swich ''unthrifty'' wayes newe. {{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 1530.}}}}

'''2.''' Not thrifty; not careful of one’s means; prodigal; profuse; lavish; wasteful.
{{smaller block|<poem>T’ inrich your selues, and your ''vnthrifty'' Sons
To Gentilize with proud possessions.</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, i. 3.}}
An ''unthrifty'' knave. {{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., i. 3. 177.}}}}

'''3.''' Not thriving; not in good condition; not vigorous in growth.
{{smaller block|Grains given to a hide-bound or ''unthrifty'' horse recover him. {{right|''Mortimer'', Husbandry.}}
At the base and in the rear of the row of buildings, the track of many languid years is seen in a border of ''unthrifty'' grass. {{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, Int., p. 3.}}}}

'''4.''' Preventing thrift or thriving; mischievous; wicked. ''Spenser'', F. Q., I. iv. 35.

'''unthrive†''' (un-thrīv′), ''v. i.'' [< ME. ''unthriven'', ''unthryven'', ''onthryven''; < ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''thrive''.] '''1.''' To fail of success.
{{smaller block|<poem>For lovers be the folke that ben on lyve,
That most disese han and most ''unthrive'',
And most enduren sorowe, wo, and care.</poem>
{{right|''Cuckoo and Nightingale'', l. 142.}} For upon trust of Calles promise, we may soon ''onthryve.''
{{right|''Paston Letters'', II. 237.}}}}
'''2.''' To fail to thrive or grow vigorously.
{{smaller block|Quyk lime, lite of that, lest it ''unthryve.''
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 122.}}}}

¶'''unthrone''' (un-thrōn′), ''v. t.'' To remove from a throne or from supreme authority; dethrone.
{{smaller block|[The Pope] Thrones and ''Unthrones'' Kings.
{{right|''Milton'', True Religion, Heresy, Schism.}}}}

¶'''untidiness''' (un-tī′di-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being untidy; lack of neatness; slovenliness.
{{smaller block|The place is the absolute perfection of beauty and ''untidiness.'' {{right|''Edinburgh Rev.'', CLXVI. 330.}}}}

¶'''untidy''' (un-tī′di), ''a.'' [< ME. ''untidy'', ''untydy'', ''untydi''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''tidy''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1†.''' Untimely; unseasonable.—'''2†.''' Improper; dishonest.—'''3.''' Not tidy; not neat; not orderly or clean.
{{smaller block|[She shall] haue mo solempne cites and semliche casteles Than ȝe treuly han smale tounes o[r] ''vntydi'' houses.
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1455.}}
She omits the sweeping, and her house and furniture become ''untidy'' and unattractive.
{{right|''Pop. Sci. Mo.'', XXXIII. 368.}}}}

¶'''untie''' (un-tī′), ''v.'' [< ME. ''unteiȝen'', ''untiȝen'', < AS. ''untīgan'', ''untīgean'', untie, < ''un-'', back, + ''tīgan'', etc., tie: see ''un-''<sup>2</sup> and ''tie''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To undo, as a knot.
{{smaller block|Bruted it was amongst the Phrygians, that he which could ''vntie'' it should be Lord of all Asia.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 326.}}}}

'''2.''' To undo the fastenings, bands, cords, or wrappings of; loosen and remove the tyings from: as, to ''untie'' a bundle; hence, to let or set loose; dissolve the bonds of; liberate.
{{smaller block|<poem>Though you ''untie'' the winds, and let them fight
Against the churches. ''Shak.'', Macbeth, iv. 1. 52.</poem>
<poem>Most haply too, as they ''untied'' him,
He saw his hat and wig beside him.</poem>
{{right|''W. Combe'', Three Tours of Dr. Syntax, i. 3.}}
All the evils of an ''untied'' tongue we put upon the accounts of drunkenness. ''Jer. Taylor.''}}

'''3.''' To loosen from coils or convolutions.
{{smaller block|<poem>The fury heard, while on Cocytus’ brink
Her snakes, ''untied'', sulphureous waters drink.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', tr. of Statius’s Thebaid, i.}}}}

'''4.''' To resolve; unfold; clear.
{{smaller block|They quicken sloth, perplexities ''untie''. ''Drayton.''}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To come untied; become loose.
{{smaller block|Their promises are but fair language, . . . and disband and ''untie'' like the air that beat upon their teeth when they spake the delicious and hopeful words.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), I. 887.}}}}

'''untied''' (un-tīd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not tied; free from any fastening or band.—'''2†.''' Figuratively, morally unrestrained; dissolute.
{{smaller block|There were excesses to many committed in a time so ''vntied'' as this was. ''Daniel'', Hist. Eng., p. 114. (''Davies.'')}}

'''until''' (un-til′), ''prep.'' and ''conj.'' [Formerly also ''untill''; < ME. ''until'', ''untill'', ''untyl'', ''ontil'', ''ontill''; < ''un-'', as in ''unto'', + ''till''<sup>2</sup>: see ''till''<sup>2</sup> and ''unto''.] '''I.''' ''prep.'' '''1†.''' To; unto: of place.
{{smaller block|Hire wommen soon ''untyl'' hire bed hire broughte.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, ii. 914.}} <poem>Also zit gert he mak tharin
Propirtese by preué gyn,
That it was like ''untill'' a heuyn.</poem>
{{right|''Holy Rood'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 123.}}}}
{{smaller block|He rousd himselfe full blyth, and hastned them ''untill.''
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. xi. 4.}}}}
'''2.''' To; unto; up to: of time.
{{smaller block|<poem>From where the day out of the sea doth spring,
''Untill'' the closure of the Evening.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. iii. 27.}}}}

'''II.''' ''conj.'' Up to the time that; till the point or degree that: preceding a clause.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Until'' I know this sure uncertainty,
I’ll entertain the offer’d fallacy.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., ii. 2. 187.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>See ye dinna change your cheer,
''Untill'' ye see my body bleed.</poem>
{{right|''Erlinton'' (Child’s Ballads, III. 222).}}}}
{{smaller block|’Tis held a great part of Incivility for Maidens to drink Wine ''until'' they are married. {{right|''Howell'', Letters, ii. 54.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Until'' that day comes, I shall never believe this boasted point to be anything more than a conventional fiction.
{{right|''Lamb'', Modern Gallantry.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>We sat and talked ''until'' the night,
Descending, filled the little room.</poem>
{{right|''Longfellow'', The Fire of Drift-Wood.}}}}
{{smaller block|The English ''until'' with the subjunctive often has a distinctly final sense, and in fact the subjunctive holds its own at that point better than at any other in English.
{{right|''B. L. Gildersleeve'', Amer. Jour. Philol., No. 16, p. 422.}}}}

'''untile''' (un-tīl′), ''v. t.'' To take the tiles from; uncover by removing tiles; strip of tiles. ''Beau. and Fl.'', Women’s Prize, i. 3.

'''untillable''' (un-til′a-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of being tilled or cultivated; barren. ''Cowper'', Iliad, i.

'''untilled''' (un-tild′), ''a.'' [< ME. ''untiled''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''tilled''.] Not tilled; not cultivated, literally or figuratively.
{{smaller block|<poem>There liues the Sea-Oak in a little shel;
There growes ''vntill’d'' the ruddy Cocheuel.</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, Eden.}}
His beastly nature, and desert and ''untilled'' manners.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Holy Dying, ii. 4.}}}}

'''untimbered''' (un-tim′bėrd), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not furnished with timber; not strongly or well timbered.
{{smaller block|<poem>Where ’s then the saucy boat
Whose weak ''untimber’d'' sides but even now
Co-rivall’d greatness? ''Shak.'', T. and C., i. 3. 43.</poem>}}
'''2.''' Not covered with timber-trees.

'''untime†''' (un-tīm′), ''n.'' [ME. ''untime'', ''untyme'', ''ontyme''; < AS. ''untīma'', ''untīme''; as ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''time''<sup>1</sup>.] Unseasonable time.
{{smaller block|A man shal nat ete in ''untyme''. ''Chaucer'', Parson’s Tale.}}

'''untimeliness''' (un-tīm′li-nes), ''n.'' The character of being untimely; unseasonableness.
{{smaller block|The ''untimeliness'' of temporal death.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', To Bishop of Rochester.}}}}

'''untimely''' (un-tīm′li), ''a.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''timely'', ''a.''] Not timely. {{smaller|(''a'') Not done or happening seasonably.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Death lies on her like an ''untimely'' frost
Upon the sweetest flower of all the field.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., iv. 5. 28.}}
It [Brook Farm] was ''untimely'', and whatever is ''untimely'' is already doomed to perish.
{{right|''O. B. Frothingham'', Reply, p. 188.}}}} (''b'') Ill-timed; inopportune; unsuitable; unfitting; improper. {{smaller block|<poem>Some ''untimely'' thought did instigate
His all-too-timeless speed. {{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 43.}}</poem>
He kindles anger by ''untimely'' jokes.
{{right|''Crabbe'', Tales, Works, IV. 8.}}}}
(''c'') Happening before the natural time; premature: as, ''untimely'' death; ''untimely'' fate.
{{smaller block|The ''untimely'' fall of virtuous Lancaster.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., i. 2. 4.}}}}

'''untimely''' (un-tīm′li), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''untimeliche''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''timely'', ''adv.''] In other than the natural time; unseasonably.
{{smaller block|Can she be dead? Can virtue fall ''untimely?''
{{right|''Fletcher'', Humorous Lieutenant, iv. 2.}}}}

'''untimeous, untimeously,''' ''adv.'' See ''untimous'', etc.

'''untimous''' (un-tī′mus), ''a.'' [Also ''untimeous''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''timous''.] Untimely; unseasonable: as, ''untimous'' hours.
{{smaller block|Of ''untymous'' persons: He is as welcome as water in a rivin ship. He is as welcome as snaw in harvest.
{{right|''Ray'', Proverbs (1678), p. 377.}}
His irreverent and ''untimeous'' jocularity.
{{right|''Scott'', Quentin Durward, I. 304.}}
[The knock] was repeated thrice ere . . . [he] had presence of mind sufficient to inquire who sought admittance at that ''untimeous'' hour.
{{right|''Barham'', Ingoldsby Legends, I. 72.}}}}

'''untimously''' (un-tī′mus-li), ''adv.'' [Also ''untimeously''; < ''untimous'' + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] In an untimous manner; untimely. ''Scott'', Kenilworth, xv.

'''untin''' (un-tin′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''untinned'', ppr. ''untinning''. To remove tin from: as, to ''untin'' waste tin-plates. ''The Engineer'', LXXI. 42.

'''untinctured''' (un-tingk′tụ̄rd), ''a.'' Not tinctured; not tinged, stained, mixed, or infected; unimbued.

{{smaller block|Many thousands of armed men, abounding in natural courage, and not absolutely ''untinctured'' with military discipline.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Nugent’s Hampden.}}}}

'''untinged''' (un-tinjd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not tinged; not stained; not discolored: as, water ''untinged;'' ''untinged'' beams of light.—'''2.''' Not infected; unimbued. ''Swift'', To Gay, July 10, 1732.

'''untirable''' (un-tīr′a-bl), ''a.'' Incapable of being tired; unwearied. ''Shak.'', T. of A., i. 1. 11.

'''untired''' (un-tīrd′), ''a.'' Not tired; not exhausted. ''Shak.'', Rich. III., iv. 2. 44.

'''untiring''' (un-tīr′ing), ''a.'' Not becoming tired or exhausted; unwearied: as, ''untiring'' patience.

'''untithed''' (un-tīᴛ̵ʜd′), ''a.'' Not subjected to tithes. ''R. Pollok.''

'''untitled''' (un-tī′tld), ''a.'' Having no title. {{smaller|(''a'') Having no claim or right: as, an ''untitled'' tyrant. ''Shak.'', Macbeth, iv. 3. 104.}}

{{smaller block|False Duessa, now ''untitled'' queene.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., V. ix. 42.}}}}

{{smaller|(''b'') Having no title of honor or office.}}

{{smaller block|The king had already dubbed half London, and Bacon found himself the only ''untitled'' person in his mess at Gray’s Inn.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Lord Bacon.}}}}

'''unto''' (un′tö), ''prep.'' and ''conj.'' [< ME. ''unto'' (not found in AS.), < OS. ''untō'', ''untuo'', ''unte'' = OFries. ''ont ti'', until, = OHG. ''unze'', ''unzi'', ''unza'', MHG. ''unze'', ''untze'' = Goth. ''unte'', up to, until; AS. ''ōth'', up to, until, < OS. ''und'', ''unt'' = OFries. ''und'', ''ont'' = OHG. MHG. ''unz'' = Icel. ''unz'', ''unuz'', ''unst'' = Goth. ''und'', up to, as far as, until; prob. another form of the prep. which appears as the prefix ''and-'', ''an-''<sup>2</sup>, and with a reversive or negative force as ''un-''<sup>2</sup>. The same first element appears in ''until'', q. v.] '''I.''' ''prep.'' To: now somewhat antiquated, but much used in formal or elevated style.
{{smaller block|Thare men gon ''un to'' the See, that schal goon ''un to'' Cypre.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 125.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A semely man to be a kyng,
A graciose face to loke ''vnto.''</poem>
{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 151.}}}}
{{smaller block|Lawes ought to be fashioned ''unto'' the manners and conditions of the people to whom they are meut.
{{right|''Spenser'', State of Ireland.}}}}
{{smaller block|God made flowers sweet and beautiful, that being seen and smelt ''unto'' they might so delight.
{{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, ii. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|Come ''unto'' me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
{{right|Mat. xi. 28.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I’ll follow you ''unto'' the death.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, i. 1. 154.}}}}
{{smaller block|They also brought a full intelligence in reference ''unto'' the particulars they were sent about.
{{right|''N. Morton'', New England’s Memorial, p. 69.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Let the North ''unto'' the South
Speak the word befitting both.</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', Texas.}}}}
'''To go in unto†.''' {{smaller|See ''go.''}}—'''To look unto.''' {{smaller|See ''look.''}}

'''II.'''† ''conj.'' Up to the time or degree that; until; till.
{{smaller block|<poem>Almighty quene, ''unto'' this yer be gon.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Parliament of Fowls, l. 647.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>In thys place abide ''vnto'' that ye see
Ho bering hym best and ho better haue.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 4131.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
